### s3-access-point-network-origin-vpc

**Claim.** An access point has a network origin of Internet or VPC. With network origin VPC, S3 rejects every request that does not come from the named VPC; the network origin is set at creation and cannot be changed afterwards.

**Scope.** per access point; fixed; set with VpcConfiguration at creation.

> "You can only specify an access point's network origin when you create the access point. After you create the access point, you can't change its network origin."

### s3-archive-restore-temporary-copy

**Claim.** Before you can access an archived object, you must restore a temporary copy of it. While the copy exists, you pay for both the archive (at the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive rate) and the temporary copy (at the S3 Standard storage rate). S3 processes only one restore request at a time per object.

> "BlockPublicPolicy | Setting this option to `TRUE` for a bucket causes Amazon S3 to reject calls to `PutBucketPolicy` if the specified bucket policy allows public access. Setting this option to `TRUE` for a bucket also causes Amazon S3 to reject calls to `PutAccessPointPolicy` for all of the bucket's same-account access points if the specified policy allows public access. <br />Setting this option to `TRUE` for an access point causes Amazon S3 to reject calls to `PutAccessPointPolicy` and `PutBucketPolicy` that are made through the access point if the specified policy (for either the access point or the underlying bucket) allows public access.<br />You can use this setting to allow users to manage access point and bucket policies without allowing them to publicly share the bucket or the objects it contains. Enabling this setting doesn't affect existing access point or bucket policies. To use this setting effectively, we recommend that you apply it at the *account* level. A bucket policy can allow users to alter a bucket's block public access settings. Therefore, users who have permission to change a bucket policy could insert a policy that allows them to disable the block public access settings for the bucket. If this setting is enabled for the entire account, rather than for a specific bucket, Amazon S3 blocks public policies even if a user alters the bucket policy to disable this setting." ### s3-block-public-access-four-settings-most-restrictive

**Claim.** Block Public Access has four independent settings (BlockPublicAcls, IgnorePublicAcls, BlockPublicPolicy, RestrictPublicBuckets) that can be applied to an access point, a bucket or a whole account in any combination. When the settings at different levels differ, S3 applies the most restrictive combination.

**Write it as.** `four settings` · `applies the most restrictive combination` · `BlockPublicAcls` · `IgnorePublicAcls` · `RestrictPublicBuckets` · `BlockPublicPolicy`

**Scope.** per access point, bucket or account.

> "Amazon S3 Block Public Access provides four settings. These settings are independent and can be used in any combination. Each setting can be applied to an access point, a bucket, or an entire AWS account."
> — [Blocking public access to your Amazon S3 storage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html)

> "If the block public access settings for the access point, bucket, or account differ, then Amazon S3 applies the most restrictive combination of the access point, bucket, and account settings."
> — [Blocking public access to your Amazon S3 storage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html)

> "IgnorePublicAcls | Setting this option to `TRUE` causes Amazon S3 to ignore all public ACLs on a bucket and any objects that it contains. This setting enables you to safely block public access granted by ACLs while still allowing `PutObject` calls that include a public ACL (as opposed to `BlockPublicAcls`, which rejects `PutObject` calls that include a public ACL). Enabling this setting doesn't affect the persistence of any existing ACLs and doesn't prevent new public ACLs from being set. Access points don't have ACLs associated with them. If you apply this setting to an access point, it acts as a passthrough to the underlying bucket. If an access point has this setting enabled, requests made through the access point behave as though the underlying bucket has this setting enabled, regardless of whether the bucket actually has this setting enabled." (columns: Name | Description)
> — [Blocking public access to your Amazon S3 storage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html)

> "RestrictPublicBuckets | Setting this option to `TRUE` restricts access to an access point or bucket with a public policy to only AWS service principals and authorized users within the bucket owner's account and access point owner's account. This setting blocks all cross-account access to the access point or bucket (except by AWS service principals), while still allowing users within the account to manage the access point or bucket.<br />Enabling this setting doesn't affect existing access point or bucket policies, except that Amazon S3 blocks public and cross-account access derived from any public access point or bucket policy, including non-public delegation to specific accounts." (columns: Name | Description)
> — [Blocking public access to your Amazon S3 storage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html)

> "BlockPublicPolicy | Setting this option to `TRUE` for a bucket causes Amazon S3 to reject calls to `PutBucketPolicy` if the specified bucket policy allows public access. Setting this option to `TRUE` for a bucket also causes Amazon S3 to reject calls to `PutAccessPointPolicy` for all of the bucket's same-account access points if the specified policy allows public access. <br />Setting this option to `TRUE` for an access point causes Amazon S3 to reject calls to `PutAccessPointPolicy` and `PutBucketPolicy` that are made through the access point if the specified policy (for either the access point or the underlying bucket) allows public access.<br />You can use this setting to allow users to manage access point and bucket policies without allowing them to publicly share the bucket or the objects it contains. Enabling this setting doesn't affect existing access point or bucket policies. To use this setting effectively, we recommend that you apply it at the *account* level. A bucket policy can allow users to alter a bucket's block public access settings. Therefore, users who have permission to change a bucket policy could insert a policy that allows them to disable the block public access settings for the bucket. If this setting is enabled for the entire account, rather than for a specific bucket, Amazon S3 blocks public policies even if a user alters the bucket policy to disable this setting." (columns: Name | Description)
> — [Blocking public access to your Amazon S3 storage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html)

### s3-change-conditional-deletes-2025-09

**Claim.** On 2025-09-16 S3 added conditional deletes in general purpose buckets: a delete sent with the if-match header and an ETag succeeds only if the ETag matches the object, and the s3:if-match condition key in a bucket policy can require the header on DeleteObject and DeleteObjects requests.

**Write it as.** `2025-09-16` · `conditional deletes`

**Scope.** general purpose buckets.

> "Amazon S3 now supports conditional deletes in general purpose buckets | Amazon S3 now supports conditional deletes in general purpose buckets. Conditional deletes verify that an object is unchanged before deleting it. Using conditional deletes helps you to prevent accidental deletions in high-concurrency, multiple-writer scenarios. You can now perform conditional deletes using the HTTP `if-match` header with an ETag value. Amazon S3 only allows your delete request to succeed if the Etag provided matches that of the object. Additionally, you can use the `s3:if-match` condition key in your S3 bucket policies to enforce conditional delete operations. For example, you can require clients to use the HTTP `if-match` header in both `DeleteObject` and `DeleteObjects` API operation requests, helping you to minimize the risk of accidentally deleting objects in your bucket. For more information, see How to perform conditional deletes. | September 16, 2025" (columns: Change | Description | Date)
> — [Document history](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/WhatsNew.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-12.

For more information, see Conditional requests. | August 20, 2024" (columns: Change | Description | Date)
> — [Document history](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/WhatsNew.html)

> "The `If-None-Match` header prevents overwrites of existing data by validating that there's not an object with the same key name already in your bucket."

### s3-cors-purpose

**Claim.** Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) defines a way for client web applications that are loaded in one domain to interact with resources in a different domain. For example, when JavaScript on a website hosted at the S3 website endpoint makes authenticated GET and PUT requests to the same bucket through its S3 API endpoint, a browser would normally block JavaScript from allowing those requests; a CORS configuration on the bucket can explicitly enable cross-origin requests from the website endpoint.

**Write it as.** `interact with resources in a different domain` · `block JavaScript from allowing those requests` · `explicitly enable cross-origin requests`

**Scope.** per bucket.

> "Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) defines a way for client web applications that are loaded in one domain to interact with resources in a different domain. With CORS support, you can build rich client-side web applications with Amazon S3 and selectively allow cross-origin access to your Amazon S3 resources."
> — [Using cross-origin resource sharing (CORS)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/cors.html)

> "A browser would normally block JavaScript from allowing those requests, but with CORS you can configure your bucket to explicitly enable cross-origin requests from `website.s3-website.us-east-1.amazonaws.com`."
> — [Using cross-origin resource sharing (CORS)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/cors.html)

> "Now you want to use JavaScript on the webpages that are stored in this bucket to be able to make authenticated GET and PUT requests against the same bucket by using the Amazon S3 API endpoint for the bucket, `website.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com`."
> — [Using cross-origin resource sharing (CORS)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/cors.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-12.

### s3-data-protection-mechanisms

**Claim.** Versioning preserves, retrieves and restores every version of every object so you can recover from unintended user actions and application failures; by default a request returns the most recently written version. Object Lock and S3 Replication are the other data protection features named beside versioning.

**Write it as.** `every version of every object` · `requests retrieve the most recently written version` · `Amazon S3 Object Lock and S3 Replication` · `recover from both unintended user actions`

> "If you make an access request to an inactive bucket, the bucket transitions to an active state, typically within a few minutes. During this transition period, reads and writes return an HTTP `503 (Service Unavailable)` error code. This doesn't apply to buckets in Local Zones."

### s3-lifecycle-small-object-default

**Claim.** Since September 2024 a Lifecycle configuration by default does not transition objects smaller than 128 KB to any storage class, because each transition is a billed request; an object size filter in the rule allows them. Before September 2024 such objects could by default transition only to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive, and configurations created before September 2024 keep that previous behavior unless you modify them.

**Write it as.** `128 KB` · `prevents objects smaller than 128 KB from being transitioned` · `add an object size filter` · `charged a transition request for each object`

**Scope.** per Lifecycle configuration; default; adjustable; an ObjectSizeGreaterThan or ObjectSizeLessThan filter changes it; configurations created before September 2024 keep the previous behavior until modified.

> "Amazon S3 applies a default behavior to S3 Lifecycle configurations that prevents objects smaller than 128 KB from being transitioned to any storage class. We don't recommend transitioning objects less than 128 KB because you are charged a transition request for each object."
> — [Transitioning objects using Amazon S3 Lifecycle](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html)

> "**Previous default transition behavior** — Before September 2024, the default behavior allowed objects smaller than 128 KB to be transitioned only to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage classes."
> — [Transitioning objects using Amazon S3 Lifecycle](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html)

> "**Updated default transition behavior** — Starting September 2024, the default behavior prevents objects smaller than 128 KB from being transitioned to any storage class."
> — [Transitioning objects using Amazon S3 Lifecycle](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html)

> "To allow smaller objects to transition, you can add an object size filter to your Lifecycle transition rules that specifies a custom minimum size (`ObjectSizeGreaterThan`) or maximum size (`ObjectSizeLessThan`)."
> — [Transitioning objects using Amazon S3 Lifecycle](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html)

> "Configurations created before September 2024 retain the previous transition behavior unless you modify them. That is, if you create, edit, or delete rules, the default transition behavior for your configuration changes to the updated behavior."
> — [Transitioning objects using Amazon S3 Lifecycle](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-12.

### s3-presigned-url-expires-with-temporary-credentials

**Claim.** A presigned URL made with temporary credentials expires when those credentials expire, even if the URL was given a later expiration time. With an assumed IAM role, the URL expires when the role session ends.

> — [Download and upload objects with presigned URLs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html)

> "A presigned URL expires at either its configured expiration time or when its associated credentials expire, whichever occurs first. For Amazon Elastic Container Service tasks or containers, role credentials typically rotate every 1-6 hours. When using AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) AssumeRole, the presigned URL expires when the role session ends, which by default is 1 hour."
